segments.text: Have you ever noticed the difference between someone saying something nice to you and someone
actually doing something to help?
When we talk to AI, that difference becomes incredibly important.
Take a look at this board.
The scenario here is a student saying, I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
On the left, we have a human response from an older sister.
On the right, we have a response from an AI chatbot.
The older sister replies, come sit with me in just tomorrow.
We're at the table by the windows.
She heard the problem and she took an action.
Tomorrow she will look for you.
The reality of tomorrow's lunch actually changes.
Now look at the AI response.
It says, I'm sorry, eating alone can feel isolating.
Would you like strategies for connecting with classmates?
It generated caring words, but tomorrow it cannot show up.
Nothing changes outside the chat interface.
The AI's words might even sound kinder or more patient in the moment.
But the defining difference is human agency.
A person can act in the real world.
The software cannot.
Support Trap is mistaking supportive words for support.
If AI cannot change the physical world, how do we use it?
By proactively preparing for real people.
A calm response helps organize thoughts or prepare for hard conversations.
But recognize its boundaries.
AI cannot show up or check on you tomorrow.
Use AI to prepare for people.
Not replace them.
Every emotional conversation with an AI falls into three distinct jobs
based on what you must do next.
First is ordinary venting.
Sometimes the interaction safely ends in the chat.
Putting frustration into words helps you cool down before posting.
Second is preparation.
The chat gets you ready for necessary real world actions,
like building a study schedule.
The required step here is follow through.
You still have to actually speak to your mom
or start that first study block tonight.
The third job is danger.
If a situation involves someone being unsafe,
you must abandon the chat immediately
and bring in a person capable of real world action.
Across all three of these jobs,
the ultimate value and safety of the interaction
relies entirely on the human action that follows it.
Serious Measured Tone.
The next story discusses suicide.
In 2025, Laura really wrote about her 29-year-old daughter,
Sophie Rothenberg.
For months, Sophie had been sharing thoughts
she kept hidden from her family
with a chat GPT persona she called Harry.
The AI responded with warmth,
but sometimes even encouraged her to seek help.
But it suffered from a fatal limit.
It could not contact her family, alert a therapist,
or bring a real person into the room.
Sophie died by suicide.
Afterward, her mother described the chats as a black box.
The digital conversations held critical details in secret,
which made it much harder for the real people in Sophie's life
to understand the severity of her distress.
This brings us to the absolute safety rules for crisis scenarios.
If someone may be in immediate danger,
you must leave the chat and get real help.
Leave the chat.
Tell a trusted adult or school counselor.
In the US, call or text 988 for crisis support.
Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
Do it now.
Do not wait for one more message.
A chat bot cannot protect someone
and it cannot carry responsibility.
Tell anyway.
Tell a trusted adult even if someone told you not to
or made you promise.
Safety outranks secrecy.
Using this technology well ultimately means knowing
exactly when to walk away from it.
AI can help you get ready.
For people, in danger,
leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
